implementation_notes: Swift's value-semantics realization is a recursive enumeration: the container case holds an array of the enum (or the enum itself is marked indirect, which inserts the pointer the compiler needs because enum values have a fixed layout), and every operation is a switch that must cover all cases. The tree is then an ordinary value that can be copied, compared and diffed, with copy-on-write making copies cheap until a node is mutated - at which point the copied path is rebuilt. Choose the protocol/class variant instead when nodes are large, mutated in place, or shared by reference.
pitfalls: Value semantics mean every mutation copies the path from the root; for large trees edited in place that cost is real and the class variant avoids it.
Without indirect (on the case or the enum) a recursive case does not compile, because enum values have a fixed layout.
Recursive functions on a deep tree can exhaust the stack; an explicit array-based stack is the escape.

variants.name: Protocol Component with reference-semantics children
variants.idiom_name: protocol Component + [any Component] children on class nodes
variants.implementation_notes: The reference-semantics realization mirrors the GoF roles: a protocol (or base class) declares the uniform operation, leaf types implement it, and containers hold [any Component] - the explicit existential spelling required since Swift 5.7 - with class nodes so children are shared instead of copied. Live UI trees (a UIView and its subviews) are exactly this shape. Pick it when nodes are long-lived, mutated in place or genuinely shared between parents; pick the indirect-enum variant when the tree behaves like a value that is rebuilt and compared.
pitfalls: Class nodes leak or cycle whenever a child keeps a strong parent reference; back-edges must be weak or unowned.
Each call through any Component goes through a witness table; hot traversals may prefer generics or the enum form.
Mutating the children array while iterating it changes the traversal - snapshot the array first.
